items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Coleman Hawkins, Ella Fitzgerald, Ray Brown, Oscar Peterson, Hank Jones, Buddy Rich, Bill Harris on trombone, Roy Eldridge, myself. ... on tour, there was Roy Eldridge one time. We had met in Cleveland many, many, many years prior to playing in New York.

ctx.x: Alright, we sort of got into Count Basie but before we do that in full swing, I just wanted to talk about your brief period in Cleveland. I guess after you were with the Earl Hood band in Columbus and other groups around there, you did do some work in Cleveland, is that right?

Yeah, I did. I went there with a band that was formerly Alphonso Trent Band. It has been quoted that I played with Alphonso Trent but I never did. He had taken ill up in New Hampshire and they took him back to Fort Smith, AR, and some of the guys kept the band together. So, they came to Columbus, that’s the first time I left Columbus was with this band. They had a trumpet player named Chester Clark and my mother told him, “Be sure and take care of my son.” He was a nice guy. I went to Cleveland with that band.…
Just to ask a little sidebar here on Emmett Berry—he’s still living…

items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Because when I first heard Dizzy he was playing exactly like Roy Eldridge.

ctx.x: You worked from nine to four?

Nine to four in the morning. And then we’d go to a restaurant or someplace and get something to eat, and then they had places where trumpet players would go. All the trumpet players, we’d all end up there. As we used to call it we’d “cut each other” all night long. I stayed in there until one or two o’clock in the afternoon you know? But what a place to be to learn your instrument. Dizzy and all of us used to do that every morning. Charlie Shavers. We’d go someplace every morning, and play. And that is like a…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: I used to go listen to ... Roy Eldridge.

ctx.x: Yeah, yeah. And then I'll never forget, while in Cleveland, McKinney's Cotton Pickers came through there. They had Roy Eldridge, Billy Bowen, Teddy Wilson, Teddy Wilson's brother Gus. Oh, man, what a band he had. What a band he had. And Clyde Hart was playing in the band. And this was later on, after the musicians I'd seen McKinney's Cotton Players -- seen with McKinney's Cotton Pickers in Columbus, they had a drummer, Cuba Austin, and all these guys, you know. But this is later in the years when Roy joined the…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: So when I started playing like that, I forgot about the Roy Eldridges and the Louie Armstrongs, you know. But always my idol -- I didn't completely forget because no one could ever forget Louie Armstrong.

ctx.x: joined Jester-Pillars, we had to play like (humming). "Doing the Continental" and all the tunes from "Stormy Weather," all the tunes from the shows. That's what we played. So to play that, you had to play with more quality, you know, Tone. They stressed that.

So when I started playing like that, I forgot about the Roy Eldridges and the Louie Armstrongs, you know. But always my idol -- I didn't completely forget because no one could ever forget Louie Armstrong. But this was a job to me and I was doing my gig. For about three years, that's all I did was play with -- around with Jester-Pillars. And when I went to New York, this is still the same style that I played, you know, in the lower register. And when I joined Basie's band, I still tried to play with this quality,…
